report:
Your “no” is reasonable for routine use: the best evidence does **not** show that coenzyme Q10 reliably relieves statin-associated muscle discomfort. The rationale is plausible—statins can lower circulating CoQ10 and muscle symptoms may involve mitochondrial pathways—but randomized-trial evidence has not translated into consistent benefit.

An updated 2018 meta-analysis of RCTs found CoQ10 did not significantly improve statin-induced myopathy despite increasing plasma CoQ10: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30371340/  
A 2020 meta-analysis of 7 placebo-controlled RCTs likewise “did not favour” CoQ10 for statin-associated myalgia, citing small samples and heterogeneity: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021915020301386  
A 2021 RCT meta-analysis concluded supplementation had no significant benefit for statin-induced myopathy: https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11845-021-02651-x  
Reflecting this, the 2018 AHA/ACC cholesterol guideline states CoQ10 is not recommended for routine use in statin-treated patients or for treating statin-associated muscle symptoms: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7403606/

Caveats: a few small or observational studies report improvement, and CoQ10 is generally well tolerated, so clinicians may consider a time-limited trial after confirming symptoms are truly statin-related. But for evidence-based relief of muscle discomfort, the answer remains no/insufficient—not a proven therapy.
